title: Side Effects, Myths and Trust
summary: Vaccines worked so well that people forgot how scary the old diseases were, and new worries grew. Scientists built "alarm systems" to spot rare problems, and they caught some real ones. They also tested a famous false claim about autism with hundreds of thousands of children and showed it was wrong.

sections.heading: The Problem with Winning, and a Sore Arm
paragraphs: By the 1980s, something odd had happened in many richer countries. Parents who had grown up in the 1950s could remember polio wards and classmates in leg braces. Their children could not. Measles, which once filled hospital beds every winter, had become rare. Diphtheria, the old "strangling angel" of children, was something you read about in history books. Vaccines had worked so well that the diseases they prevented had nearly vanished from everyday life.

That success created a strange new puzzle. When a disease is all around you, the danger is easy to see and a sore arm seems like nothing. When the disease has disappeared, people stop weighing the vaccine against the illness, because they have never seen the illness. Instead, all they notice is the needle, the crying baby and any worry they hear about. Public-health experts sometimes call this the "victim of its own success" problem.

This part of the story is about side effects, scary rumours, real mistakes and the question of trust. It is a story about how scientists check claims, how safety systems spot rare problems, and why some fears turned out to be true while others were false. It is not a guide to what any reader should do. Questions about anyone's own health always belong with a doctor and trusted adults.
So let's begin with a simple question that turns out to be surprisingly interesting: what actually happens to most people after a vaccination?

The most common side effects of vaccines are small and short. The place where the needle went in can become sore, red or a little swollen. Some people feel tired, get a headache, ache a bit or run a mild fever for a day or two. Babies may be grumpy and sleepy. These effects usually fade within a few days.

Here is the surprising part: many of these effects are signs that the immune system is doing its job. Remember from earlier parts how the immune system raises the alarm when it meets something new. Immune cells rush to the spot, release chemical messengers and turn up the body's "thermostat". That is why a vaccine can cause a little of the same tiredness and warmth you feel at the start of an illness, without the illness itself.

Rarer reactions exist too. The one that clinics are most prepared for is a sudden, severe allergic reaction called anaphylaxis. For most vaccines it happens roughly once in every million doses, which is why people are often asked to wait a short while after a vaccination, and why clinics keep medicine ready to treat it quickly. Fainting is another reaction that sounds dramatic but is usually caused by nerves about the needle rather than the vaccine, especially in teenagers.

Scientists are careful to say that no vaccine is perfectly free of side effects, and no vaccine protects 100 per cent of people. What they try to measure, as accurately as possible, is how often each problem happens and how that compares with the harm the disease itself would cause. To measure something that might happen once in a million times, you need a very big net. That net is the vaccine safety monitoring system.

sections.heading: Alarm Bells: How Safety Systems Work
paragraphs: Even the biggest clinical trial, with tens of thousands of volunteers, cannot spot a problem that happens once in 100,000 or once in a million people. Only when millions of people receive a vaccine does a very rare effect have a chance to show up. That is why safety checking does not stop when a vaccine is approved. It carries on for as long as the vaccine is used. Scientists call this post-marketing surveillance, or "Phase 4".

Britain was one of the first countries to build such a system for all medicines. In 1964, still shaken by the thalidomide disaster, in which a medicine taken during pregnancy caused serious harm to thousands of babies around the world, the UK launched the Yellow Card scheme, developed by the doctor Bill Inman. Today it is run by the Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency (MHRA). Anyone, from a doctor or pharmacist to a patient or parent, can send in a report of a suspected side effect.

In the United States, the Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System, or VAERS, began in 1990. It grew out of a law passed in 1986, the National Childhood Vaccine Injury Act, and is run jointly by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Like the Yellow Card scheme, it is open to everyone. It is designed as an early-warning system: a smoke alarm rather than a fire investigator.

That difference really matters. A report to VAERS only says "this happened after a vaccination". It does not prove the vaccine caused it. Imagine that a million children are vaccinated on a Monday. By pure chance, some of them will catch a cold, fall off a bike or develop an illness they were going to get anyway in the following week. Some of those events will be reported. So when a pattern appears, scientists ask a sharper question: is this happening MORE often than we would expect if there were no vaccine at all? They compare the number of reports with the normal "background rate" of that illness.

To answer such questions properly, the CDC also runs the Vaccine Safety Datalink, set up in 1990 as well. It links the electronic health records of several large health-care organisations (13 member sites today), so researchers can compare vaccinated and unvaccinated people, or people in the weeks just after vaccination with the same people at other times. Many other countries, such as Denmark and Finland, have national health registers that allow similar checks on whole populations. Together these systems have caught real problems, as the next two stories show.

sections.heading: When the Alarms Were Right: 1976 and 1999
paragraphs: In February 1976, soldiers at Fort Dix, an army base in New Jersey, fell ill with a respiratory infection. Tests showed a type of swine flu virus (H1N1) that seemed related to the virus behind the terrible 1918 flu pandemic. One young soldier, Private David Lewis, died, and about a dozen others were taken to hospital. Health officials were frightened that a giant pandemic might be starting.

The US government launched a huge programme to vaccinate everyone. President Gerald Ford rolled up his sleeve for the cameras. Starting in the autumn of 1976, about 43 to 45 million Americans were vaccinated in just a few months. But the feared pandemic never came: the virus did not spread beyond Fort Dix. Meanwhile, reports began to arrive of Guillain-Barré syndrome, a rare condition in which the immune system attacks the nerves, causing weakness that most people recover from slowly. The CDC later estimated that the swine flu vaccine added roughly one extra case for every 100,000 people vaccinated. On 16 December 1976 the programme was stopped and never restarted. Some researchers have since questioned how strong the link was, but the episode taught health officials hard lessons about speed, communication and watching closely.

The second story concerns rotavirus, a germ that causes severe diarrhoea in babies and at that time killed hundreds of thousands of young children every year around the world. In 1998 the first rotavirus vaccine, called RotaShield, was licensed in the United States. Its trials had shown it worked well. But once it was in wide use, reports reached VAERS of a rare bowel problem called intussusception, in which part of the intestine slides into the next part like a folding telescope and becomes blocked. CDC investigators found the risk rose in the week after the first dose, by about one extra case for every 5,000 to 10,000 babies vaccinated.

Within about a year of licensing, in 1999, the recommendation was withdrawn and the maker took RotaShield off the market. The next rotavirus vaccines, RotaTeq (approved in the United States in 2006) and Rotarix, were tested in much larger trials designed specifically to look for this rare problem before approval. These two stories show something important: the safety net is not just for show. When it finds a real signal, vaccines are paused, restricted or withdrawn.

sections.heading: Rare Signals in a Pandemic
paragraphs: The same kind of watching happened again, on a gigantic scale, when COVID-19 vaccines were rolled out from December 2020 (their creation is the story of the next part). Because billions of doses were given within months, problems far too rare for any trial to detect could finally be seen.

In March 2021, doctors in Europe noticed a small number of unusual cases among people who had recently received the Oxford-AstraZeneca vaccine. A few people had developed blood clots in unusual places, such as veins draining the brain, together with a low number of platelets, the tiny blood cells that help blood clot. The condition was given a long name: vaccine-induced immune thrombotic thrombocytopenia, or VITT. It was later also linked to the Johnson & Johnson (Janssen) vaccine, which was built in a similar way. It was very rare, roughly one or two cases per 100,000 doses in the figures reported by Germany and the UK, but it could be serious.

Countries reacted in different ways. Denmark stopped using the AstraZeneca vaccine. Germany and the Netherlands kept it mainly for people over 60. The UK offered younger adults, first under 30 and later under 40, a different vaccine. Australia preferred another vaccine for adults under 50. Doctors also learned how to recognise and treat VITT quickly. Researchers pointed out that the same kind of brain clot was several times more common after COVID-19 infection itself than after the vaccine, which is the sort of comparison regulators weigh up.

A different rare effect was found with the mRNA vaccines made by Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna: myocarditis, an inflammation of the heart muscle, and pericarditis, inflammation of the thin bag around the heart. It appeared mostly in teenage boys and young men, usually a few days after the second dose. Regulators estimated the overall risk at about one case per 100,000 people vaccinated, higher in young males. Most cases were mild and people recovered quickly with rest and treatment. Information leaflets were updated, and some countries adjusted the gap between doses or which vaccine they offered to young men. Once again, the system had seen a real signal and responded.

sections.heading: The Paper That Fooled the World
paragraphs: Not every scare comes from a real signal. The most famous false alarm in vaccine history began on 28 February 1998, when the respected British medical journal The Lancet published a paper led by a London doctor named Andrew Wakefield. It described just 12 children with bowel problems and developmental conditions, and suggested a possible link between the MMR vaccine (measles, mumps and rubella) and autism.

Twelve children is a tiny number, and the paper itself did not prove anything. But at a press conference Wakefield suggested that parents might choose single, separate vaccines instead of the combined MMR. Newspapers and television ran the story for years. Many parents, understandably wanting to protect their children, became frightened.

Then a journalist, Brian Deer, began investigating. Over several years he discovered that Wakefield had serious conflicts of interest that he had not declared, including payments linked to lawyers who were preparing to sue vaccine makers. Deer also found that details of the children's histories had been changed to fit the story the paper told. In 2004 most of Wakefield's co-authors withdrew their support for the paper's interpretation.

On 2 February 2010, The Lancet fully retracted the paper, which means it officially withdrew it as untrustworthy. Its editor, Richard Horton, said that claims in it were "utterly false". In May 2010 Britain's General Medical Council found Wakefield guilty of serious professional misconduct, and he was struck off the UK medical register, so he can no longer work as a doctor there. In January 2011 the British Medical Journal published Deer's findings with an editorial calling the original paper "an elaborate fraud". Wakefield has continued to deny wrongdoing, but the scientific verdict is clear: the paper was dishonest, and vaccines do not cause autism.

sections.heading: How Scientists Check a Claim
paragraphs: How can scientists be so confident? Not by trusting one expert, but by testing the idea again and again in huge groups of people. Here is the reasoning. If MMR caused autism, then children who had the vaccine should be diagnosed with autism more often than children who did not. That is something you can count.

First, a word about autism itself. Autism is a difference in how a person's brain develops, affecting how they communicate, sense the world and interact with others. Autistic people are as varied as anyone else, and many describe autism as simply part of who they are. Researchers have found that genes play a large part, and that the brain differences linked to autism begin developing before birth. Part of what made the vaccine scare so hurtful was that it treated autism as damage someone must be blamed for. Major scientific bodies, including the US Institute of Medicine, the World Health Organization, the FDA and the CDC, all reviewed the evidence and rejected the idea that vaccines cause it.

Denmark is especially good at this kind of counting, because every person has an ID number linked to health records. In a study published in 2019 in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine, Anders Hviid and colleagues followed 657,461 Danish children born between 1999 and 2010, adding up to more than 5 million "person-years" of watching. Children who received MMR were not more likely to be diagnosed with autism than children who did not. That stayed true even in groups thought to be at higher risk, such as children with an autistic brother or sister. A 2014 review combining studies of more than 1.25 million children found the same thing, and so have many other studies in different countries.

Why did the myth feel believable to so many people? Partly because of timing. The first signs of autism are often noticed by parents in a child's second year of life, which is also when the MMR vaccine is usually given. When two things happen around the same time, our brains easily link them, even when one did not cause the other. Scientists have a phrase for this: correlation is not causation. Large studies are a way of escaping that trap.

A related worry concerned thimerosal (also spelled thiomersal), a preservative containing a form of mercury that was used in some multi-dose vaccine vials to stop bacteria and fungi growing. In July 1999 American health authorities said they had found no evidence of harm from the tiny amounts in vaccines, apart from occasional skin reactions, but asked manufacturers to remove it from children's vaccines as a precaution. By 2001 it had been taken out of, or reduced to trace amounts in, routine US childhood vaccines. If thimerosal had been causing autism, diagnoses should have dropped afterwards. Instead, autism diagnoses kept rising, which researchers link mainly to wider definitions and better recognition of autism.

This is how science is supposed to work. A claim was made, it was taken seriously, and it was tested over and over by independent teams. The answer kept coming back the same. Scientists also stress that questioning is healthy: asking "how do we know?" is exactly what led to these studies in the first place.

sections.heading: When Measles Came Back
paragraphs: Fear has real effects. In the UK, the share of young children receiving MMR fell from about 92 per cent in 1996 to about 84 per cent by 2002, and in some parts of London it dropped to around 61 per cent. Remember from part 11 that measles is so contagious that around 95 per cent of people need to be immune to stop it spreading. Gaps in protection let it back in. Recorded measles cases in the UK rose from 56 in 1998 to hundreds a year by the mid-2000s, and in 2008 measles was declared endemic again, meaning it was circulating steadily within the country. In Ireland, an outbreak in 2000 caused about 1,500 cases and three children died.

The United States had declared measles eliminated in 2000, meaning it no longer spread continuously within the country. But travellers can bring it in, and where groups of unvaccinated people live close together, it spreads. In 2019 the US recorded 1,274 confirmed measles cases across 31 states, the largest number in decades. Preliminary CDC figures show 2,289 cases in 2025 and 4,852 by 29 October 2026, as outbreaks grew again.

Why do health officials worry so much about a disease that many people remember as a childhood rash? Measles spreads through the air when an infected person coughs or sneezes, and the virus can hang in a room for up to about two hours after they leave. Most children recover, but some develop pneumonia or swelling of the brain, and a small number die, especially babies and children who are poorly nourished. Measles can also weaken the immune system's memory of other germs for months or years afterwards, a finding scientists sometimes call "immune amnesia". This is why a rise of a few percentage points in unprotected children can turn into hundreds or thousands of cases.

In 2019 the World Health Organization listed "vaccine hesitancy", which it defined as reluctance or refusal to vaccinate despite vaccines being available, as one of ten threats to global health. WHO said vaccination prevents about 2 to 3 million deaths a year and that about 1.5 million more could be avoided if coverage improved. It also noted that the reasons for hesitancy are complicated: some people feel the diseases are no longer a danger (complacency), some find it hard to get to a clinic, and some lack confidence in vaccines or in the people offering them. Health workers in local communities, WHO found, are the voices people trust most.

sections.heading: Trust, History and the Hard Question of Rules
paragraphs: Trust is not just a feeling. It is built, or broken, by how people have been treated. One of the darkest examples in American medicine is the Tuskegee syphilis study, which was NOT a vaccine study but still shapes how many people feel about medical research. From 1932 to 1972, the US Public Health Service followed 600 poor Black men in Macon County, Alabama, 399 of whom had syphilis. The men were never told their diagnosis, and even after penicillin became the standard cure in the 1940s they were not given it. A Public Health Service worker, Peter Buxtun, raised the alarm, and a news story by reporter Jean Heller exposed the study in July 1972. It was stopped that year. In 1997 President Bill Clinton formally apologised to the survivors.

The scandal led to new rules. The National Research Act of 1974 and the Belmont Report of 1979 set out principles that now guide research on people: respect, informed consent, fair treatment, and review of every study by an independent ethics committee before it can start. Historians and researchers have found that the revelations deepened mistrust of medicine among many Black Americans, a mistrust with roots in earlier abuses too. Remembering such history helps explain why some people ask hard questions, and why honesty and fairness matter so much in public health.

Then there is the oldest argument of all: should vaccination ever be required by law? As part 6 described, England made infant smallpox vaccination compulsory in 1853, protests followed, and in 1898 parents gained the right to object on grounds of conscience. In 1904 a smallpox vaccination law in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, set off days of rioting known as the Vaccine Revolt. In 1905 the US Supreme Court heard the case of Henning Jacobson, a pastor in Cambridge, Massachusetts, who had refused smallpox vaccination during an outbreak and been fined 5 dollars. In Jacobson v. Massachusetts the court ruled 7 to 2 that a state could require vaccination to protect public health, while noting that courts could step in for a person who would be harmed by it.

Today, countries make very different choices. All US states require certain vaccinations for children to attend school, but most allow some exemptions, and the rules keep being debated. Australia in 2016 linked some family benefits to children's vaccination records, with exemptions for medical reasons. In 2021 the European Court of Human Rights decided that the Czech Republic's childhood vaccination requirement did not break human-rights law. Other countries rely only on recommendations and free clinics. People who value personal freedom and people who focus on protecting the community, especially those who cannot be vaccinated, have argued about where to draw the line for more than 170 years. This book will not tell you the answer; it is a question societies keep working out together.

By the end of 2019, the picture was mixed. Vaccines were saving millions of lives a year, safety systems were watching closely, and science had answered the biggest myths. Yet trust was wobbling in many places. Then, in the first days of 2020, doctors in Wuhan, China, began reporting cases of pneumonia caused by a new coronavirus. Within weeks it was spreading across the world, and humanity needed a vaccine faster than it had ever made one before.

deepDive:
Vaccine safety science is mostly a problem of rare events and big numbers. A Phase 3 trial of 30,000 to 40,000 people can reliably detect side effects that occur in roughly 1 in 1,000 to 1 in 10,000 recipients, but not ones at 1 in 100,000 or 1 in a million. A rough rule of thumb (the "rule of three") says that if no cases of an event are seen among N people, you can be about 95 per cent confident its true rate is below 3 in N. So a 40,000-person trial with no cases still allows a risk of up to about 1 in 13,000. That is why passive reporting systems (VAERS, Yellow Card) and active systems (the Vaccine Safety Datalink, Nordic national registers) are essential after approval.

Passive systems are sensitive but noisy. Anyone can report, so reports include coincidences, duplicates and, sometimes, entries filed for lawsuits. Analysts therefore look for "disproportionality": an event reported more often after one vaccine than after others. A signal is then tested with designs that control for chance and bias, such as the self-controlled case series, which compares the same individuals in a "risk window" just after vaccination with other times, cancelling out personal factors like genetics. This is how the RotaShield intussusception risk (about 1 in 5,000 to 10,000) and the mRNA myocarditis risk in young males were pinned down.

The MMR-autism question shows the other side of the coin: proving a negative as far as science can. No study can prove a risk is exactly zero, but the Danish cohort of 657,461 children produced a hazard ratio of 0.93 with a 95 per cent confidence interval of 0.85 to 1.02. In plain words, any hidden effect would have to be extremely small, and the best estimate is no effect at all. Combined with other cohorts totalling well over a million children, the evidence is about as strong as epidemiology can provide.

Researchers who study hesitancy describe the "3 Cs": confidence (trust in vaccines and the system), complacency (feeling the disease is not a threat) and convenience (how easy it is to get vaccinated). Debates about mandates turn on ethics as much as data: how to balance personal liberty against harm to others, and whether incentives, exemptions or education work best. Different democracies have reached different answers, and the evidence on which policies raise coverage is still argued over.
funFact: The famous 1905 US Supreme Court case about compulsory vaccination, Jacobson v. Massachusetts, began with a fine of just 5 dollars.
